newsitem.title: USA: Annan goes to Washington to heal UN-USA wounds.
newsitem.headline: Annan goes to Washington to heal UN-USA wounds.

text.p: United Nations chief Kofi Annan arrived in Washington on Wednesday hoping to convince his critics the United States needs to pay its debts to the world body and that he is committed to wide-reaching reform.

The trip follows at least two years of relentless U.S. criticism of the United Nations as a body that is too powerful and wasteful of funds. For Annan, it is a "time for healing," a veiled reference to the scorn heaped on the United Nations and his predecessor, Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt, driven from office by the Clinton administration at the end of a five-year term.
"War is the failure of diplomacy, therefore diplomacy is the first line of defence," the new secretary-general said, adding he hoped to convince Washington to invest in diplomacy.

The soft-spoken 58-year-old Ghanaian, who took office on Jan. 1, will try to convince leading senators and members of Congress that the United States needs the United Nations and vice versa. And that means paying the $1.3 billion debt owed by Washington that has crippled the world body.

"He has only a few months to cement the relationship and get the United States to really take its place among U.N. members and not shoot from the sidelines," one senior official said. "It is a healing time but not a long one."

U.S. President Bill Clinton has proposed paying the debt by 1999, with some conditions attached. But whether the Republican-dominated Congress, which cut non-defence foreign aid to a bare minimlum, will agree is another question.

Annan on Thursday was to see Clinton, Secretary of State-designate Madeleine Albright and National Security Adviser Sandy Berger, among others. In a bid to improve U.N. relations with Congress, he also has meetings planned with a host of legislators including House of Representatives Speaker Newt Gingrich, Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott and North Carolina Sen. Jesse Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The wide gap between Democrats and Republicans was illustrated clearly in Helms' article in Foreign Affairs magazine six months ago in which he advocated the United States withdraw from the United Nations unless its budget was slashed more than anticipated so far.
Annan has touted reform as a top priority and plans wide-ranging proposals in the next six months. But he pointedly said reform did not mean massive or "arbitrary" cuts in vital programmes.
Some nations, such as Japan, believe reform should not mean any lowering of dues but the release of funds for development to poor countries.

Since many U.N. bodies are not under the control of the secretary-general but are funded by voluntary contributions, Annan's influence on wide-ranging restructuring is often dependent on approval by member states.

But since the Clinton administration faulted Boutros-Ghali for allegedly not paying enough attention to reform, Annan was left with an albatross of massive change in order to get the United States to participate fully in the United Nations.
"It is up to the member states to define what they want the United Nations to be and to do -- to outline their vision of the goals they want us to attain and to set new priorities," he said.
